articles.title: First day of Ukraine peace talks constructive, Zelensky says
articles.snippet: Delegations from Kyiv, Washington and Moscow are in the United Arab Emirates for the first trilateral talks since February.
articles.full_text:
First day of Ukraine peace talks constructive, Zelensky says
- Published
The first of two days of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine has concluded in Abu Dhabi.
While senior officials from Kyiv and Moscow were tight-lipped after the four hour-long discussions, President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was not at the talks, said they had proved "constructive and quite substantive".
Speaking from Paris, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said the meeting had been "very productive".
Although expectations for a breakthrough that ends Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine are low, US officials said earlier that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would control Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario.
Zelensky also said that humanitarian issues such as prisoner of war exchanges had been discussed.
At the start of Tuesday's talks President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, told delegates that the US had "narrowed the gaps" between the two sides, without providing details, and hoped to move towards a "solution that hopefully ends the war".
Kushner had said earlier the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.
He and Trump peace envoy Steve Witkoff also met Ukrainian and European and Nato officials on the sidelines of the main meeting.
Until now European leaders have largely been excluded from peace talks, but they have pushed to be included in the discussions amid concerns that decisions about their continent's security would be made without them.
The Americans appear to support this, with Rubio acknowledging during a visit to Paris that the Europeans "are a part of solving this problem for the long term".
However, "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans", according to a US official.
Some proposals favoured by EU officials - such as calling an unconditional ceasefire as a prerequisite for peace negotiations - are routinely rejected by Moscow. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Tuesday that a truce would just allow Kyiv to regroup. "We will not agree to it," he said.
Moscow and Kyiv's positions are still far apart on ending the conflict.
A key area of disagreement involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia.
Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are crucial to its future security.
While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately".
However, he acknowledged the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture".
"They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other."
For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it comes under attack again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from Eastern Europe â which would be alarming to Europeans.
The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022.
The last round of trilateral talks, held in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough. Soon after, the US-Israel war on Iran diverted Washington's attention from Ukraine, and no other discussions were held since.
From the start of his second term in office, US President Donald Trump â who once boasted he could end the war in Ukraine within a day â has spearheaded several rounds of talks to end the conflict, albeit with little success.
Meanwhile, his increasingly conciliatory approach towards Moscow has fuelled deep unease in Kyiv and across the European Union.
After meeting Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev in Washington last week, Trump touted a forthcoming "big, beautiful agreement" on Ukraine that "might involve all of Europe".
Many in Ukraine are sceptical that this would result in a fair peace.
Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the foreign affairs parliamentary committee, told the BBC he believed Trump wanted "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine", which will certainly be rejected by Kyiv.
The only way to make Russia's Vladimir Putin start real negotiations was by putting greater pressure on Russia through sanctions and deep strikes, Merezhko said.
"While Putin has a war machine up and running, he has no incentives to negotiate." He also mentioned recent moves by Trump, such as his deal to buy diesel from Russia, as something that "only encourages Moscow to continue the war".
Moscow's delegation in Abu Dhabi includes Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yury Zhigarlovsky.
Kyiv has sent several senior officials who have been part of previous negotiating teams, including Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, and MP Davyd Arakhamiya.
Away from Abu Dhabi, Russia continues to pummel Ukraine with deadly bombardments and strikes on energy infrastructure, viewed in Kyiv as proof that Moscow wants to corner Ukraine into accepting a deal on Russia's terms.
On Monday, Kushner was cautious to point out that the Abu Dhabi talks could at most "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations".
"This is an extraordinarily difficult and complicated conflict," he wrote on X, adding the US was "approaching these discussions with determination and realism."

articles.title: Arrests made in Mohamed Al Fayed probe in France, police say
articles.snippet: The Ritz hotel in Paris, which is still owned by the Al Fayed family, is one of the properties searched by police.
articles.full_text:
Arrests made in Mohamed Al Fayed probe in France, police say
- Published
French police have made arrests after three properties, including the Ritz hotel in Paris, were searched in relation to an investigation into Mohamed Al Fayed's abuse.
The Paris prosecutor's office told the BBC that several individuals were taken into custody for questioning last month and later released.
In a confidential letter sent to survivors, the Metropolitan Police said its officers were present during the searches on 13 and 14 October, in what is understood to be a joint operation between British and French authorities.
It is the first time any arrests have been made in relation to alleged abuse and trafficking by the former Harrods and Ritz owner.
Mohamed Al Fayed accused of multiple rapes by staff
- Published19 September 2024
Several victims of Al Fayed were also interviewed by French investigators, the prosecutor's office said.
It added that the searches were part of a preliminary investigation into "allegations of human trafficking committed by an organized group, aggravated pimping committed by an organized group, and rape".
The investigation is ongoing and digital material seized during the searches is being analysed.
The late Egyptian billionaire bought the Ritz Paris hotel in 1979, and it is still owned by the Al Fayed family.
The Villa Windsor in western Paris, another property involved in the search, was a holiday home for the Al Fayed family. It was previously the home of King Edward VIII, following his abdication, and his wife Wallis Simpson.
The Met shared this statement from French authorities with victims:
"At this stage of the proceedings, several victims have been interviewed by French investigators, and the investigations are being conducted in liaison with the British authorities.
"In this context, searches and evidence-gathering operations were carried out in mid-October 2026, notably within the Hotel Ritz in the 1st arrondissement of Paris, as well as at the Villa Sainte-ThÃ©rÃ¨se in Saint-Tropez, a former property of Mohamed Al Fayed, and at the Villa Windsor in the 16th arrondissement of Paris, in the presence of British investigators.
"Several suspects were taken into police custody, measures which were lifted following their interviews, specifically for the purpose of analyzing digital material seized during the search operations.
"The investigations are continuing under the direction of the Paris Public Prosecutor's Office."
A Met Police spokesperson confirmed its officers travelled to France in October and were present during the operation.
Al Fayed, who died in 2023 aged 94, was accused by more than 20 women of sexual assault in a BBC documentary and podcast in September 2024.
One of the women featured in the documentary said she was sexually assaulted by Al Fayed at the Ritz hotel in Paris, while another woman said she had been raped by him at the Villa Windsor residence.
Since those allegations, more than 400 alleged victims or witnesses have come forward to lawyers.
A woman has also told BBC Scotland she was trafficked, drugged, sexually assaulted and held prisoner on the Balnagown Estate by Al Fayed's brother, Salah Fayed, who died in 2010.
Both brothers died without facing legal charges in relation to these allegations.
Earlier this year, Police Scotland said it was carrying out further investigations into allegations connected to Balnagown Estate.
In a statement, a force spokesperson said: "Three people have been identified in connection with offending against a number of victims.
"Our inquiries are ongoing and it would be inappropriate to comment further."
The Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors group said it welcomed the "significant developments" and cooperation between the Met and French authorities.
"We believe that all properties owned by Fayed should be investigated with the same thoroughness as those already searched, wherever they are located, to ensure that no potentially relevant evidence is overlooked," the group said.
"We hope these developments represent meaningful progress towards identifying and holding to account all those who facilitated, concealed or assisted his offending, wherever they operated."
The survivor advocacy group No One Above said: "France is treating this as organised human trafficking, led by specialists, with properties searched and evidence seized. That is what a serious investigation into a network looks like.
"Two years on, survivors are still waiting for the same from the Met. It is time the National Crime Agency took this investigation over."
The management of the Ritz Paris told AFP news agency that it "does not tolerate any form of harassment, abuse or inappropriate behaviour" and that it was ready "to cooperate fully with the competent judicial authorities".
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support is available at BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Israel's new parliament sworn in as leaders compete to form government
articles.snippet: Benjamin Netanyahu's main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, has first chance to build a new government and oust the prime minister.
articles.full_text:
Israel's new parliament sworn in as leaders compete to form government
- Published
Israel's new parliament has been sworn in, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The former army chief has been tasked with forming a government after receiving more recommendations from members of the Knesset than Netanyahu, although not all those backing him are willing to govern together.
Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in October's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. He has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension.
Almost half of the new MKs did not serve in the previous parliament, while Arab-led parties have a record number of seats.
Shortly after they were sworn in, Netanyahu and Eisenkot warned parliament about the perils of supporting a government led by the other.
"[And] to those who are thinking of establishing a government that includes supporters of terror and haters of Israel, or that will be dependent on them, I ask you, are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?" said Netanyahu, alluding to the prospect of an Eisenkot-led government reliant on support from Arab parties.
He also appealed for the formation of a government of national unity as the only way to confront what he said was the threat of "a nuclear Iran".
Eisenkot sharply criticised Netanyahu's comments.
"I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister's delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech, exploiting a state occasion," he said. "I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute."
The outcome of the election, which was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, means there is a period of uncertainty over who will form the next government. Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until then - a process which could take from days to months.
One of the most dramatic results was the performance of Israel's two Arab-led alliances - the United Arab List and the Joint List - which won an unprecedented 19 seats between them following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
The Arab parties could therefore hold the balance of power, although Netanyahu has ruled out governing with them and three of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc have opposed including them in a coalition.
On Sunday, President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with trying to form a government.
Speaking at the president's residence, the centrist Yashar party leader called for the formation of a "national emergency government" - an implicit appeal to parties to put ideological differences aside to remove Netanyahu from office.
This, he said, would "require creative and unconventional political steps".
Eisenkot said any party or MK prepared to accept four principles could join his proposed government. Those are recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state; accepting the values of the Declaration of Independence; backing mandatory military, national or civilian service for all, including communities currently exempt; and recognising Hamas as a terrorist organisation and committing to dismantling its military and governing capabilities.
The four requirements, however, could present significant obstacles to Eisenkot's potential partners.
The conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, who are exempt from military service if they are in full-time religious study, was a major election issue.
The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas parties, which won 13 seats in total, have fiercely objected to attempts to change the status quo - something that all parties in Eisenkot's bloc campaigned to do.
Eisenkot's four principles are also contentious for the Arab parties. Both emphasise equal national and civic rights for Israel's Arab citizens, who form about 20% of the population; the vast majority of Israeli Arabs are not required to serve in the military; and neither has publicly recognised Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
The Arab parties could, though, help Eisenkot form a minority government. The United Arab List, which won eight seats, has said it is willing to be part of an Eisenkot-led coalition, while the Joint List, which won 11 seats, has offered parliamentary support from the outside.
If Eisenkot accepted such an arrangement, he would still have to persuade other parties in his bloc to agree. Avigdor Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beiteinu party won seven seats, has so far refused to join a minority government dependent on Arab MKs.
In return for their support, the ultra-Orthodox parties would be likely to demand major concessions on military conscription, which might be unacceptable to most of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc.

Police officer dies and another injured after backpack explosion in northern Spain
- Published
A police officer has died and another has been injured in the northern Spanish city of Oviedo after an explosive device went off at the scene of a shooting.
The blast happened when officers from Spain's canine unit and explosives disposal unit arrived and examined a suspicious backpack following reports of a dispute between neighbours on Tuesday morning.
A woman who had been shot and the injured officer have been taken to hospital for treatment.
The suspect fled the scene and is still at large, police said.
Spanish police paid tribute to the dead officer, who has been named as Juan JosÃ©, in a statement on X and said: "Our hearts are with his family, friends, colleagues and loved ones."
Officers attended the scene early after receiving reports of an argument between neighbours and upon arriving found a woman who had sustained gunshot wounds, police spokesman Pedro Aguado said.
While searching for the suspected attacker, officers found a suspicious backpack with a flashing light and contacted both the bomb disposal unit and canine unit.
"While the package was being moved outside to ensure the safety of the residents, an explosion occurred," Aguado added.
The explosion left a member of the canine unit dead and an officer from the bomb disposal unit seriously injured, he said.
A three-year-old police dog named Deny was also killed in the explosion.

articles.title: Anti-homosexuality laws in Trinidad and Tobago overturned
articles.snippet: The ruling brings to an end an 11-year legal battle by dual-citizen Jason Jones.
articles.full_text:
Anti-homosexuality laws in Trinidad and Tobago overturned
- Published
A UK court has overturned laws criminalising same-sex intimacy in Trinidad and Tobago.
London's Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC), the Caribbean island's final court of appeal, ruled the laws were not in keeping with the "fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life."
The judgement is the result of an 11-year legal battle brought by dual-citizen Jason Jones, 62, who said he hoped it would "accelerate the fight for full equality."
Jones had successfully challenged the laws in 2018 in Trinidad's High Court, however the ruling was overturned on appeal by the Trinidadian government.
It is the first time the JCPC has ever decided on a case to decriminalise same-sex intimacy, and campaigners hope it will spark similar successful legal challenges elsewhere in the Commonwealth.
Prior to this historic decision, Trinidad and Tobago was one of some 34 Commonwealth countries continuing to criminalise homosexuality based on colonial-era British laws.
Under these laws, consensual same-sex intimacy is punishable by imprisonment, and in some cases carries the death penalty.
The Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago had argued that the law was protected from legal challenges by the "savings law clauses" - which carried over existing British laws into newly independent states.
Representatives for Jones argued that the laws violated an individual's right to privacy and argued the government's changes to the laws in 1986 - which saw stricter punishments introduced - meant the savings clause protections no longer applied.
The judicial committee unanimously found in favour of Jones.
Handing down the judgement, Lord Sales told the court the laws "cannot be regarded as reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of an individual".
Jones, human rights campaigner and appellant in the appeal, said: "These laws never reflected who we are as a people and a nation - diverse, multiracial, and secular.
"They told LGBTQ+ people that we were criminals in our own country. That message ends today."
Lawyer Anand Ramlogan SC, representing Jones, said the judgement was a "landmark victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago."

articles.title: French wartime resistance heroine Solange Alexandre dies aged 104
articles.snippet: With 30 men under her orders, she organised sabotage operations, sheltered Allied airmen and joined the fight against the occupying German forces.
articles.full_text:
French wartime resistance heroine Solange Alexandre dies aged 104
- Published
One of France's last Resistance heroes from World War Two has died at the age of 104. Solange Alexandre was also a rare woman who, with her future husband, created and commanded her own unit of anti-German fighters.
After serving as a Resistance courier from 1941, three years later she founded the Pas-de-Boeuf network near the town of RuillÃ©-sur-Loir.
With some 30 men under her orders, she organised sabotage operations, sheltered Allied airmen and, after the Allied landings in Normandy on D-Day in 1944, joined the fight against the occupying German forces.
President Emmanuel Macron was among many to pay tribute to Alexandre, after her death was announced at a nursing home in Le Mans.
"She said she only ever did her duty. But her duty was our freedom. France will never forget. Thank you," Macron posted on social media.
Born in 1922 in the Sarthe department of western France, Solange Alexandre, nÃ©e Dubuisson, grew up in a patriotic family that had suffered in World War One.
"My mother lost her first husband in the war, and my father was wounded in 1917. The words homeland and honour were very important to us. They were in my blood," she recalled in her memoirs.
In June 1940 she heard on the radio the appeal from General Charles de Gaulle in London, calling on the French not to give up the struggle against Germany. She had never heard of him, but that did not matter.
"From that moment I knew I had to join up," she wrote.
Some months later she was recruited by a friend of her father's â a Tunisian-born French army veteran called SaÃ¯d Belhaffaf, who had joined the Resistance.
Using the code-name Corlay, she criss-crossed the region around Le Mans by bicycle, gathering information and passing on messages.
"There were no mobile phones back then, and no private cars either because of the lack of petrol. The bicycle was king," she said in an interview two years ago.
In 1943 she met her first husband Guy DÃ©liot, who had deserted from the French gendarmerie after refusing to arrest some Jews.
The following April, with the Allied invasion approaching, they decided to take to the maquis, in other words live clandestinely in the forested hills, supplied with food by local farmers.
Their group consisted of deserters from German forced labour programmes, as well as survivors from another Resistance outfit that had been destroyed by the enemy. There were also two airmen, one American and one Canadian.
"Twice the Gestapo came for me, and twice I slipped through their hands," she later recalled.
After taking part in the liberation of Tours in September 1944, she ended the war with the rank of sub-lieutenant in the French Interior Forces (FFI).
Later she worked as a teacher and followed her husband on his many postings as an officer of the gendarmerie in French overseas territories. He was killed in 1960 in Martinique, and in 1981 she remarried.
Twice Solange Alexandre turned down the LÃ©gion d'Honneur, saying that she had only done her duty and that others were more worthy.
Finally in 2024 she relented.
On receiving the award she said: "It is a great pleasure and a great honour. I am very proud â even if it is only a few weeks, or a few months, before I die."

articles.title: Twelve dead after motorway pile-ups in Bulgaria fog
articles.snippet: About 50 other people were injured in the pile-ups along a section of the Trakia motorway, officials have said.
articles.full_text:
Twelve dead after motorway pile-ups in Bulgaria fog
- Published
Twelve people have been killed after dozens of cars and lorries were involved in two pile-ups on the Trakia motorway in south-eastern Bulgaria, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said.
Health Minister Katya Ivkova said 11 people died at the scene on Tuesday, near the town of Zimnitsa, while another person later died in hospital. About 50 others were taken to hospital with injuries.
Sliven regional governor Mihail Kasherov told journalists that more than 70 vehicles were involved in the incident, Bulgarian state news agency BTA reported.
Officials have said dense fog reduced visibility and was the likely cause of the first crash, which occurred on the eastbound carriageway.
Radev declared Wednesday a day of national mourning following the incident.
The second crash, on the Sofia-bound carriageway, was likely also caused by the fog, with drivers also distracted by the first crash, BTA reported an official as saying.
The Trakia motorway runs from west-to-east of Bulgaria, and connects the capital Sofia to the Black Sea coast.
Road administration director Galin Kostov added that speeds were unsuitable for the conditions, which included wet road surfaces, and the motorway would remain closed until it had been cleared, BTA reported.
Yambol regional governor Georgi Chalakov said reports first came in at 07:10 local time (05:10 GMT), with the injured taken by ambulance to hospitals in the Yambol, Sliven and Burgas regions.
Chalakov told BTA rescue teams had to remove sections of the crash barrier to reach people. He added that the fog meant that helicopters could not be used in the evacuation efforts.
One witness who helped rescue a man from a burning vehicle blamed "very thick fog" for the pile-up.
"I got out of the car, I ran forward and pulled that man out," the witness told Reuters news agency.
Another told Reuters that "many, many people died".
"As for me, there were four cars behind me - trucks - and I don't know how I got out or what happened, but in the end, thank God I'm still alive," that witness said.
Radev - who had been hosting European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen - cut short a news conference after learning of the incident and visited the scene.

articles.title: US federal authorities could have prevented Epstein crimes, report finds
articles.snippet: The report by a Republican-led congressional committee follows a 15-month investigation into the handling of the late disgraced financier's case.
articles.full_text:
US federal authorities could have prevented Epstein crimes, report finds
- Published
Crimes committed by the late disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein after 2005 could have been prevented were it not for "failures" by federal investigators and prosecutors, a congressional investigation has concluded.
The Republican-led US House Oversight Committee on Tuesday released its final report into what it described as the "decades-long" mishandling of the criminal investigations into Epstein and his long-term associate Ghislaine Maxwell.
The report's findings are based on interviews and depositions with witnesses, government files, and financial records over a 15-month period.
Epstein died in 2019 as he awaited trial on sex trafficking charges.
"While some of these failures involved an exercise in poor judgement by the USAO, others appeared to be the result of Epstein's pervasive and wide-reaching influence," the report reads, referring to the US Attorney's Office.
It states that, rather than fully investigating allegations in other states, the USAO for the Southern District of Florida entered an agreement with Epstein in 2007 allowing him to evade federal prosecution.
Regarding Epstein's death in a New York prison, investigators concluded this was a result of "a series of institutional failures at the facility," which included staffing shortages, overworked employees, poor recordkeeping, and lax security practices.
Testimony the panel solicited was "unable to definitively dispel certain theories" surrounding Epstein's death, the report states, including accounting for a lapse in surveillance footage.
It found the justice department (DoJ) failed to communicate about document releases and that deficient redactions exposed survivors' sensitive personal information.
Earlier this year, the DoJ had to remove thousands of documents related to Epstein from its website after victims said their identities had been compromised.
The report also alleges that financial institutions like American Express enabled human trafficking and immigration fraud, by allowing Epstein to use decoy flights and dummy itineraries to transport foreign workers across borders. The BBC has contacted American Express for comment.
The investigative panel recommended that Congress should pass legislation to prevent the weaponisation of non-disclosure agreements, which they said Epstein used to silence survivors.
"Epstein operated with impunity, shielded and enabled by powerful connections and a justice system that repeatedly failed his victims," said James Comer, the Republican chairman of the committee.
He called upon the DoJ to "interview or re-interview key witnesses, investigate Epstein associates accused of criminal activity, and ensure survivors have access to their records.
The report accuses Democrats of being "obsessed" with trying to implicate US President Donald Trump and that an "unfounded witch hunt continued without regard for the interests of survivors".
Trump has previously said he was friendly with Epstein before they fell out in 2004. The president's name has appeared thousands of times in the Epstein files but there is no suggestion that appearing in the documents implies any wrongdoing.
The committee's review of documents did not identify any that would implicate Trump, the report concluded.
In a statement, Rep Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the Oversight Committee, alleged his Republican colleagues "released a report based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings on Jeffrey Epstein".
Garcia accused the justice department of withholding "over 2.5 million pages of documents".
"We will not allow the President and his allies to dismiss this investigation," said Garcia, who is expected to lead the committee when Democrats take control of Congress in January following the recent midterm elections.
- Published23 April

articles.title: Myanmar summons German envoy over controversial video
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Mathias Licharz calls for the 'unconditional' release of ousted politicians, including former leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
articles.full_text:
Myanmar summons German envoy over controversial video
Mathias Licharz calls for the ‘unconditional’ release of ousted politicians, including former leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
Myanmar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has summoned the head of mission at the German embassy in the country over a Facebook video calling for authorities to “unconditionally release” ousted politicians such as former leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
The ministry said in a statement on Tuesday that Mathias Licharz in the video “appeared to fuel opposition to the host country and its Government, thereby inciting internal unrest”.

Licharz met Deputy Foreign Minister Ko Ko Kyaw, was “warned against the video” and handed an aide-memoire, the ministry said.
“The Deputy Minister strongly warned against recurrence of such act and informed him that any similar conduct would be treated with utmost seriousness and would take appropriate actions,” the ministry said.
Licharz posted the video on Sunday, standing outside the former Yangon residence of Win Myint, the figurehead president of Aung San Suu Kyi‘s government that was removed in a 2021 coup.
The German diplomat said in his message, marking Win Myint’s 75th birthday, that the United Nations still regards him as the “legitimate president” of Myanmar.
In the video, he called for authorities to “unconditionally release all those who are arbitrarily detained, including Win Myint and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi” – using the affectionate term by which Aung San Suu Kyi‘s supporters refer to her.
Germany’s embassy in Myanmar did not immediately comment.
Win Myint’s downfall
Win Myint was jailed in the February 2021 military coup, ending Myanmar’s decade-long democratic experiment.
Since then, pro-democracy rebels rose up and long-simmering ethnic minority rebellions challenging central rule boiled over.
Authorities said in April he had been pardoned of his post-coup convictions – charges that supporters and analysts say were confected to oust the government.
However, Licharz said in his video message his efforts to meet Win Myint had been unfruitful.
“There is only one conclusion,” he said. “U Wint Myint is not a free man. He’s not allowed to meet with whom he would like to meet, and he’s not allowed to communicate independently,” he added, using a male honorific.
The military leadership behind the coup organised elections, installing a nominally civilian government this year, although analysts regard it as a fig leaf for ongoing military rule.
“Should the Charge d’Affaires choose to recognize U Win Myint as President and wish to discontinue his service in Myanmar, the Ministry would have no objection,” the Foreign Ministry statement said on Tuesday.
Aung San Suu Kyi remains detained but was moved to house arrest in the capital Naypyidaw this year, authorities say, where access to the 81-year-old Nobel Peace Prize laureate remains tightly controlled.

articles.title: Photos: Crowds greet Pope Leo in Argentina after 40-year wait
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Pope Leo XIV urges Argentinians to emulate their saints during his landmark visit, drawing crowds not seen for decades.
articles.full_text:
In Pictures
Photos: Crowds greet Pope Leo in Argentina after 40-year wait
Pope Leo XIV urges Argentines to emulate their saints during his landmark visit, drawing crowds unseen for decades.
Pope Leo XIV has urged Argentinians to follow the “holy example” of the country’s saints and build a more “fraternal and caring nation”, as an estimated 650,000 people packed the central city of Cordoba for Mass.
The 71-year-old pontiff, on a 12‑day Latin America tour less than a month after lung cancer surgery, on Tuesday celebrated the liturgy on the esplanade of a military aircraft factory.
The Vatican said it was attended by 650,000 pilgrims, following Monday’s Mass in Buenos Aires, where about 2.5 million worshippers gathered – the largest of his pontificate so far.
In Cordoba, Leo listed Argentinian saints and blessed figures as examples of a unity “between passion for the Gospel and commitment to building a fraternal and caring nation”, urging citizens to evangelise “at school and in the square, in the family and with friends, in the countryside and in the city, at the dairy farm and in the office”.
Faithful travelled from across the country after nearly 40 years without a papal visit. “It was quite a journey,” said Erika Vinales, who travelled 2,000km (1,242 miles) from Patagonia with fellow teacher Elena Llanquenao.
Throughout his three days in Argentina, Leo has repeatedly challenged President Javier Milei’s right-wing government to make the economy more inclusive, protect trade unions and reverse funding cuts that hurt the poor and people with disabilities.

Inflation remained high, despite some easing in fuel prices caused by the US war on Iran.
Consumer prices in the United States increased in October more than expected, even as petrol prices fell to a four-month low after some easing of concerns about the long-term impact of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on global markets.
In its latest report released on Tuesday, the US Department of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Statistics said the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for all items rose by 0.4 percent in October, continuing an inflationary trend since July. The average cost of shelter, as well as food, also rose in October, according to the agency.

The Labor Department’s report was higher than the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, which had forecast the CPI to increase by 0.2 percent, and economists polled by FactSet, who had predicted an increase of 0.3 percent, despite the lowering pressure on energy prices.
On Monday, US President Donald Trump said that future military action against Tehran was unlikely. “Iran militarily is effectively over,” Trump said. “We’re just keeping it the status quo, and we’re doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours.”
The average price of a gallon of petrol fell below $4 ($1.06 per litre) for the first time since July, according to the American Automobile Association. The economy and cost-of-living concerns were leading concerns for voters in midterm elections that were held on November 3, which saw Republicans lose control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on the eve of the elections found that 78 percent of voters said cost-of-living was very important or the most important issue for them when considering how they would vote. How voters view Trump himself has also turned largely negative since the war and its impact on the economy. Only 32 percent of voters approved of his job performance, according to the Reuters/Ipsos poll, just one point above his record low of 31 percent last month.
Trump’s Republican Party was dealt major losses in the midterm elections, losing typically Republican seats in Congress in states like Texas and Kansas.
Trump himself, as well as key members of his administration like Vice President JD Vance, have acknowledged that the war on Iran played a part in those electoral losses.

articles.title: Iran backs nuclear treaty even as hardliners raise prospect of bomb
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Iran says it is committed to non-proliferation treaty, but hardliners may be pushing for a change in nuclear policy.
articles.full_text:
Iran backs nuclear treaty even as hardliners raise prospect of bomb
Iran says it is committed to non-proliferation treaty, but hardliners may be pushing for a change in nuclear policy.
Tehran, Iran – Iran says it has not suspended its commitments under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), but as mediated talks to end the war with the United States continue, broad international inspections of Iranian sites remain far off.
Following US and Israeli attacks on Iran’s main nuclear facilities in and assassinations of senior leaders, Iranian authorities have increasingly discussed the possibility of abandoning the international treaty and building a nuclear bomb.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3‘Another round of war less likely’: Momentum builds for peace in Iran
- list 2 of 3Hegseth impeachment: What is he accused of, and could he be removed?
- list 3 of 3What is Shahid Kaveh, the Iran cyberunit tied to France’s fridge hacking?
US President Donald Trump’s threats to attack the underground Pickaxe Mountain complex near the Natanz nuclear facility and other sensitive sites have only emboldened hardliners in Tehran to demand a shift in the country’s nuclear doctrine – under assassinated Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, nuclear weapons were officially forbidden.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei emphasised to reporters during a news conference in Tehran on Monday that the Islamic Republic remains committed to the NPT, despite restricting cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the United Nations’ nuclear watchdog.
“Other parties have imposed conditions, namely the attacks by the US and Zionist regime against our nuclear facilities which have caused issues concerning implementation of safeguards commitments,” he said, in reference to Israel.
“As long as this situation continues, we cannot act like normal circumstances in our cooperation with the agency,” Baghaei said about the IAEA, while also renewing Tehran’s criticism of its director, Rafael Grossi.
But the spokesman confirmed that new IAEA inspections were conducted days earlier at the Bushehr nuclear power plant.
The electricity generation plant, built in cooperation with Russia and under development for new phases, is the only facility still accessible to the agency, as it was not directly bombed during the war. US warplanes did, however, attack the perimeter of the plant several times and caused damage, prompting partial evacuation of Russian personnel, who have yet to fully return.
IAEA chief Grossi told the UN Security Council in late October that the body was unable to verify Iran’s nuclear material because Tehran “has not provided the requested information and access”.
Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa programme at the International Crisis Group, said Tehran is keeping one foot inside the NPT and the other near the exit.
“Allowing inspections at Bushehr is a low-cost gesture designed to keep diplomacy alive and hardliners at bay, while preserving leverage over the underground nuclear sites that matter most,” he told Al Jazeera.
Those sensitive sites include the Natanz, Fordow and Isfahan facilities, among others.
Seyed Hossein Mousavian, a visiting researcher at Princeton University and a former Iranian nuclear negotiator, said Iran’s position “reflects a distinction between honouring its NPT commitments and permitting inspections of facilities that have been bombed”.
Mousavian said the IAEA had no established inspection protocol for nuclear facilities damaged by military attacks, and pointed out that the Iranians fear that IAEA access to sensitive sites would lead to information being shared with the US and Israel that could then be used in future attacks.
“Tehran views restrictions on broader inspections as a security concern rather than necessarily a rejection of its NPT obligations,” he said.
Nuclear commitments and benefits
Iran has had one of the most scrutinised nuclear programmes in history, and its international obligations are governed by several treaties and UN resolutions.
The NPT establishes the fundamental rules against nuclear proliferation, while recognising the right to peaceful nuclear energy. A separate safeguards agreement with the IAEA sets out how the agency monitors Iran’s nuclear activities to make sure it isn’t moving towards weapons development. Subsidiary arrangements, UN Security Council resolutions and nuclear agreements have fulfilled additional requirements.
As a party to the NPT, Iran’s peaceful nuclear-use rights are recognised, and it is allowed to undertake peaceful exchanges and receive assistance with nuclear development.
In exchange, the country commits not to receive, manufacture or otherwise acquire nuclear weapons, and to accept safeguards and information sharing in its territory.
Withdrawal requires a notice after a decision has been made that “extraordinary events” have “jeopardised the supreme interests” of the country.
However, the treaty does not protect from conventional military attack, and this gap between promised peaceful-use benefits and actual vulnerability has been at the centre of the appeal by domestic hardliners to leave the NPT.
But such considerations have not been limited to a handful of hawkish figures.
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei has publicly deliberated the possibility of abandoning the treaty on multiple occasions. Hossein Mohebbi, spokesman of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said earlier this week that the organisation “will create the necessary preparations” if the Islamic Republic goes through with the decision to change its nuclear doctrine.
Negotiations ongoing
Regional mediators like Qatar and Pakistan continue to relay messages between Iran and the US to prevent another all-out war, although analysts have warned that escalation is likely over the coming months.
Tehran has maintained that it will not allow its highly enriched uranium to be taken out of the country, but remains open to downblending it under international supervision inside Iran. It has also said it will not abandon enrichment altogether, but can accept a limit on enrichment as it did with the 2015 nuclear deal that US President Donald Trump unilaterally abandoned in 2018, during his first term in office.
Arriving at a deal that thoroughly addresses Iran’s nuclear programme would also require a resolution to hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz and beyond, something that is unlikely to materialise in the foreseeable future.
“Tehran might be willing to open the door a crack in exchange for tangible American concessions, but it is unlikely to surrender its most valuable nuclear bargaining chips upfront,” the Crisis Group’s Vaez said.
The expert added that a preliminary deal could potentially unlock limited, phased inspections based on the 2025 Cairo agreement between Iran and the IAEA.
The agreement came several months after the US and Israel bombed Iran’s nuclear facilities during the 12-day war of June 2025. It envisaged restored access for agency inspectors to all Iranian facilities, if case-by-case permission is granted by the country’s Supreme National Security Council.
But it was never enforced, and was followed by tensions that led to the US and Israel attacking Iran again on February 28.
“Restoring meaningful transparency over Iran’s nuclear programme will require a larger bargain on enrichment, stockpiles and sanctions relief,” Vaez said.
But Mousavian said Tehran would want more than just a preliminary agreement like the Cairo deal.
“Such cooperation would require a comprehensive agreement that addresses the overall security and nuclear issues; without it, inspections of the bombed sites are unlikely,” he said.

Anthropic targets $1.4 trillion valuation in massive stock market debut
The maker of Claude is looking to raise up to $64.4bn in one of the largest IPOs in history next week.
Anthropic is seeking a valuation of $1.4 trillion for its upcoming IPO, with the company looking to raise as much as $64.4bn in what would be one of the largest stock market debuts in history.
The company, which makes the Claude AI chatbot, launched its investor roadshow on Tuesday, with reported plans to go public next week.

According to its filing with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Tuesday, Anthropic plans to offer 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78, giving it a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion when potential shares are included.
It has also secured $26bn in a separate private placement backed by some of the world’s largest tech companies, including Google, Nvidia, Microsoft and AMD.
The listing is being closely watched as a major test for how much investors are still willing to bet on AI companies, which have driven huge gains in tech stocks and the broader US market.
The $1.4 trillion valuation is lower than earlier estimates, which had suggested Anthropic could be valued between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion, as concerns grow about the company’s enormous infrastructure spending and recent swings in AI stock prices.
Those concerns extend beyond Anthropic, with investors increasingly questioning whether AI companies can make enough money to justify their soaring valuations and sustain the boom.
Despite the uncertainty, Anthropic’s growth has been explosive.
The company reported revenues of $17bn in their third quarter, up from $1.4bn a year earlier, as its net losses narrowed. On Tuesday, Anthropic said it was on pace to generate about $81bn in annual revenue, $10bn higher than its estimate a month earlier.
The company credits its growth to the demand for Claude, including from industries like healthcare, financial services and legal services.
But to keep up with that demand, Anthropic has committed almost $900bn to computing costs with partners including Amazon and Google, a massive financial bet on continued demand for its product.
The IPO also lands in an uncertain political climate, with Democrats having just won control of both chambers of the US Congress in the midterm elections last week. The new Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate have raised the prospect of more regulation of AI companies and new restrictions on the construction of data centres that power the technology.
AI stocks slid after the midterms, with the Nasdaq falling 5.5 percent on Thursday, its biggest one-day drop in more than a year. The selloff, also driven by declines at Nvidia, whose CEO was targeted by an alleged Chinese spy, wiped out trillions of dollars from the market.
Markets have since recovered some of those losses, though the Nasdaq dipped slightly below 1 percent on Tuesday. Some analysts argued the sell-off was an overreaction and that the election was unlikely to derail the expansion of data centres.

articles.title: Pentagon can’t track millions of F-35 spare parts, watchdog finds
articles.snippet: The GAO reported that while the DoD's F-35 program "is the costliest in its history," the department "struggles to account" for its parts.
articles.full_text:
The Pentagon is still struggling to track millions of F-35 spare parts worth billions of dollars years after government watchdogs first exposed problems with its tracking system, a new report states.
The Government Accountability Office said Monday that while the DoD’s F-35 program “is the costliest in its history,” the department “struggles to account” for its parts.
The government watchdog described the DoD’s records for F-35 parts as “outdated, inaccurate, and incomplete” and said “DoD has made minimal progress in attaining and maintaining accountability for F-35 parts” since issues were first brought to light seven years ago.
The report follows several audits since 2019 by the GAO and the Department of Defense Inspector General, which revealed numerous problems.
Unlike most aircraft, the F-35 program largely relies on a joint pool of spares – such as engines and tires – for the U.S. Air Force, Navy and Marine Corps, as well as international customers.
As of March 2026, this pool comprised approximately 26 million spare parts valued at around $31 billion, the GAO reported. About 17,000 parts – worth up to $2.5 billion – were not recorded in the Pentagon’s property and logistics management platform, the Enterprise Logistics Management System.
In 2023, the GAO reported that one prime contractor lost more than 1 million F-35 spare parts worth more than $85 million from 2018 to 2022. As of March 2026, the F-35 Joint Program Office still did not know the status of the items.
The F-35 has two prime contractors: Lockheed Martin for the airframe, and Pratt & Whitney for the engines. The U.S. Air Force awarded Lockheed Martin a $1.6 billion contract for more spare parts in July.
Issues still plague inventory tracking systems used by the F-35 Joint Program Office.
“For instance, records of F-35 parts in the F-35 program’s accountable property system of record remain unreliable, since they do not reflect real-time changes and are inaccurate and incomplete,” the GAO report states.
Nor can the Enterprise Logistics Management System track joint spare parts in real-time “because ELMS does not currently interface with the two prime contractors’ property management systems.”
“DoD does not have its own complete records of F-35 parts, and, as a result, does not know when a part is lost unless staff at the contractor-managed or government-managed facility identifies and reports the loss,” Asif Khan, director of GAO’s financial management and assurance team, told Defense News.
For joint spares, the F-35 Joint Program Office relies on data supplied quarterly by the prime contractors, which means that “joint spares pool data in ELMS may be more than 3 months old.” Whether some F-35 spares are actually located where they should be isn’t always clear, in part because the prime contractors aren’t always aware of inventories held by their subcontractors.
Some parts were also valued quite cheaply in the contract data requirements lists, which are submitted by the prime contractors quarterly.
“Almost 6 percent of records of F-35 parts, also from the December 2025 CDRL, showed an acquisition cost of $0.01 or less, also indicating a possible data quality error,” the GAO noted.
“Neither records of F-35 parts in ELMS nor F-35 JPO’s inventory results are reliable for the purpose of asset accountability or financial reporting,” the report states.
Even estimating how many of the 26 million F-35 parts are missing is difficult.
“Because the F-35 JPO has not established and implemented effective procedures for monitoring losses, we are unable to provide an aggregate estimate of how many of the 26 million parts are lost,” Khan said.
The F-35 Joint Program Office should improve its procedures for recording lost parts, “including procedures for performing trend analyses that would enable mitigation of future losses,” the GAO recommended. The office should also make more use of accountable property officers who maintain records of parts, including specific training focused on the F-35 program.
Questions remain about whether an inability to track spare parts is hampering F-35 operations.
The GAO warned earlier this year that poor parts accountability is complicating efforts to improve the F-35 program. Customers have also been asking for greater transparency into the supply chain so they can properly allocate resources, Khan noted.
“For several years, we’ve been reporting that DoD cannot ensure that the prime contractor is providing sufficient readiness at a reasonable cost without an understanding of the parts it owns and how the prime contractor manages those parts,” Khan said.

articles.title: Pentagon can’t track thousands of F-35 parts: GAO
articles.snippet: The government watchdog found that more than 17,000 F-35 fighter jet parts worth an estimated $1.3 billion were missing from the program’s inventory system.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The F-35 Joint Program Office cannot reliably track thousands of spare parts undergoing maintenance or repair, leaving officials without a clear picture on the location of as much as $2.5 billion worth of components across the aircraft’s global supply chain, according to a new government watchdog report.
The Government Accountability Office’s findings come against the backdrop of a Pentagon investigation into how F-35 components shipped from Australia to the United States ended up in Hong Kong, potentially exposing the jet’s secrets to the Chinese government. While GAO did not link the incident to inventory problems detailed in the report, the watchdog’s findings underscore the Pentagon’s broader challenges in tracking F-35 parts.
As of March 2026, when the GAO conducted its research, more than 17,000 F-35 Lightning II parts, worth an estimated $1.3 billion, were missing from the program’s inventory system. The value could be as high as $2.5 billion when accounting for missing cost information and other acquisition expenses, officials told GAO.
The gaps stem in part from incomplete contractor records that are not routinely integrated into the program’s inventory system, making it difficult for the JPO to determine what parts are available and where they are.
“Without accurate data in its [accountable property system of record] and properly executed inventory procedures for F-35 parts, DOD management will not have the information it needs to support warfighter readiness and reliable financial reporting,” the GAO said.
The F-35 comes in three primary variants that are operated by the Air Force, Marine Corps and Navy, as well as specialized configurations for 19 international customers. Lockheed Martin serves as the stealth fighter’s prime contractor, while RTX subsidiary Pratt & Whitney supplies its engine.
Overall, the F-35 program relies on over 1,900 domestic and 2,100 global suppliers, with approximately 26 million parts distributed across more than 700 contractor- and government-management facilities worldwide, per the GAO. The Defense Department uses the Enterprise Logistics Management System (ELMS) to manage the fighter jet’s sprawling inventory.
While the ELMS is able to capture real-time inventory changes, the platform cannot interface with property management systems run by Lockheed Martin and Pratt & Whitney — an issue first reported by GAO in 2022, which has persisted as of August 2026, according to the watchdog.
Instead, the JPO relies on periodic contractor data submissions and information from other Pentagon systems to update its records. Those submissions occur quarterly for the joint spare parts pool, meaning some inventory records can be more than three months old, GAO found.
Furthermore, the JPO lacks procedures to validate the accuracy of contractor data before entering it into the ELMS. A December 2025 submission included serial numbers for only 29 percent of parts records and National Stock Numbers for 43 percent. Some of those records indicated the components cost just one cent or less, which GAO said indicated possible data errors.
The program office has also struggled to verify how many F-35 parts are at facilities. Since fiscal 2020, the JPO has spent at least $17 million conducting inventories, but GAO found that its most recent effort did not fully verify that parts were physically in place or that inventory records accounted for all of them.
A JPO spokesperson told Breaking Defense that it was “actively working” to address the issues raised in the GAO report, including development of new procedures and training for officials responsible for government-owned property, while working to better monitor and analyze parts losses.
“The JPO is modernizing its property management infrastructure by establishing direct, real-time data interfaces between government and prime contractor systems. This integration directly addresses previous system gaps to ensure seamless accountability of F-35 spare parts,” the spokesperson said in a statement.
Lockheed Martin deferred all questions regarding the GAO report to the F-35 JPO, but told Breaking Defense that the company is focused on improving the stealth fighter’s readiness, affordability and sustainment.
“We work closely with the F-35 Joint Program Office, U.S. services, international customers, and industry partners to improve parts availability, repair turnaround times and supply chain performance,” a Lockheed spokesperson said in a statement. “The proposed multiyear procurement and sustainment framework, subject to congressional authorization and appropriations, would provide greater predictability for suppliers to plan and invest in production and repair capacity.”
An Ongoing Concern
The report echoes concerns the watchdog has raised in previous reviews of the Pentagon’s costliest program. In 2023, GAO found that a prime contractor had lost more than 1 million F-35 parts worth over $85 million between May 2018 and October 2022.
By March 2026, the contractor had submitted about $28 million in loss reports covering the missing parts between 2012 and 2025. The Defense Contract Management Agency determined the contractor should be financially liable for about $6 million, but the JPO could not determine whether those reports included any of the losses identified in GAO’s earlier review because it had not kept records of outstanding cases, according to the latest report.
The accounting problems could also affect the Pentagon’s ability to keep the F-35 ready for operations, GAO warned. Without accurate inventory records, the department may struggle to determine which parts it needs and in what quantities.
That could complicate the Pentagon’s $13.7 billion Global Support Solution Reset strategy, which calls for additional investment to improve F-35 performance — including increasing spare parts availability. The watchdog cautioned that the Pentagon may be unable to identify its needs or account for additional parts purchased under the strategy.
In the report, GAO recommended that DoD strengthen its oversight of reported parts losses and establish clearer procedures, training and responsibilities for officials who track government-owned property. The Pentagon agreed with all four recommendations and said it was taking corrective actions.
The Defense Contract Audit Agency is also working with the JPO on a full inventory of F-35 parts, targeted for completion in March 2027.

articles.title: Report: Russian ships are pumping tanks, MRAPs and rocket launchers into Africa
articles.snippet: Russian cargo ships have carried military equipment including tanks, armored vehicles and rocket launchers to African ports serving as gateways to Moscow’s forces on the continent, according to a new investigation.
articles.full_text:
VIENNA — Russian cargo ships have carried military equipment including tanks, armored vehicles and rocket launchers to African ports serving as gateways to Moscow’s forces on the continent, according to a new investigation that also identifies a possible additional supply route through the Republic of Congo.
The data collected by C4ADS, a Washington-based organization that tracks illicit networks globally, spans the past three years and includes a sample of a dozen ships with operational ties to Russian military shipments. The analysts used open-source information including AIS ship transponder data, satellite imagery, on-the-ground pictures and local reporting to track the ships’ journeys between 2023 and 2026.
The ports of Conakry, in Guinea; Tobruk, in Libya; and Lomé in Togo were particularly important for Russian logistics likely in support of Moscow’s Africa Corps troops. The Corps, which is under Russia’s Defense Ministry, grew out of the former Wagner Group, a paramilitary force that operated across Africa and beyond on behalf of the Kremlin’s great power politics. Mali, which C4ADS researchers suggest may have been the ultimate destination for many of the weapons shipped, is a particular Africa Corps hot spot.
The analysts tracked five known military-affiliated transport ships going from Russian Baltic and Arctic ports to Conakry between December 2024 and March 2026, from where military convoys then continued inland to Mali.
Among the ships calling at Conakry were the Adler and Siyanie Severa, which arrived in January 2025. “Within days, a convoy of roughly a hundred military vehicles, including Spartak mine-resistant ambush protected (MRAP) armored vehicles and T-72 heavy tanks, was filmed arriving in
Bamako,” the capital of Mali, C4ADS said in a write-up shared with Defense News ahead of the investigation’s publication.
Similar voyages were observed by other ships at later dates, including the Baltic Leader and Patria, which arrived in Conakry in May of the same year, after which more MRAPs appeared in the region. The pair of ships was accompanied by a third, the Siyanie Severa, which continued past Conakry to Bata, Equatorial Guinea and Lagos, Nigeria.
Some of the cargo ships to Africa are escorted by Russian navy ships for part or all of their voyages, such as the Sabetta, which arrived in Conakry in March 2026 after being escorted by a warship through the English Channel. C4ADS said the ship likely delivered military equipment, including Tigr infantry mobility vehicles, to Africa on that trip.
In addition to known Russian arms shipment routes, the researchers specialized on illicit network detection said that the port of Pointe-Noire in the Republic of Congo may have emerged as a new logistics hub for Russia’s military operations in Africa.
The American analysts identified three U.S.-sanctioned ships designed specifically for vehicle transport traveling from the Black Sea and St. Petersburg areas to Congo between 2023 and 2026, two of which also made voyages to West African ports that are more firmly known to be affiliated with Russian weapons shipments in the same timeframe. The researchers noted that more work was needed to conclusively determine the nature of shipments to Pointe-Noire.
Meanwhile, Libya featured as a regular destination; Russia’s Africa Corps is reportedly heavily involved in the eastern half of the country, a region that is controlled by General Haftar’s Libyan National Army.
“Like shipments to West Africa, deliveries to Libya follow a recurring pattern: departure from Baltiysk Naval Base in Kaliningrad, a naval escort indicating high-value cargo, and
frequent prolonged AIS signal gaps in the Mediterranean,” C4ADS said, calling out a tracking obfuscation technique that is also frequently used by Russia’s shadow fleet of tankers.
With regard to Togo, analysts assessed that the country had become a significant waypoint for Russian supply routes into the Sahel following a 2025 military cooperation agreement signed between Moscow and Lomé. Ships docking at the port were assessed as delivering war materiel to Mali by way of Togo and Burkina Faso.
The researchers said the cargo ship Mikhail Britnev likely carried military vehicles and equipment to Lomé in June and July 2026. Malian state television subsequently showed a convoy of 29 armored vehicles in Bamako that reporters said had traveled from Lomé.
Russian involvement in Africa is not new, dating back to the Soviet era and reinvigorated by the Wagner Group in the 2010s. The maritime routes complement an air logistics network previously investigated by Defense News, with Russian military-affiliated cargo aircraft operating through Algeria and onward to other African destinations.
C4ADS says that ten of the twelve vessels it tracked are U.S.-sanctioned, compared with six covered directly or through their owners by British sanctions and five by European Union sanctions.
The report, including an interactive map, will be released to the public on Nov. 10.

articles.title: Hegseth denounces ‘farce’ impeachment in first briefing since May
articles.snippet: Hegseth argued the impeachment articles brought forth Monday were a politically motivated "farce" directed at service members.
articles.full_text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday vehemently defended himself against impending impeachment proceedings, conflating accusations against his actions with disrespect for the troops and listing off military successes in his first Pentagon press briefing in over six months.
Hegseth focused on the Pentagon’s victories Tuesday, alternating between throwing jabs at former officials and praising President Donald Trump. The conference lasted fewer than 25 minutes, and he answered few questions from the gallery.
Hegseth said the impeachment articles — brought forth Monday by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie — constitute a politically motivated “farce,” directed at service members.
“Politicians in Washington have accused the sailors and pilots who struck narcoterrorist boats of war crimes for doing their job,” he said, later equating his own impeachment possibility with potential repercussions for service members. “This resolution is the next step. Put the secretary on trial today and then men and women who carried out those orders tomorrow.”
Hegseth painted himself as a champion for the troops, saying, “If they want to come for the warriors, they’re going to have to come through me.”
The proceedings came shortly after Republicans’ massive losses in the midterm elections, which Vice President JD Vance blamed on the war in Iran. Hegseth addressed Vance’s comments, saying that the war was “a necessary undertaking.”
Hours after Hegseth’s conference, Vance took to social media in support of the defense secretary, calling the question of whether Hegseth carried out impeachable offenses “absurd,” and saying that “impeachment has become a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking.” Vance said lawmakers were targeting Hegseth because he “took on bureaucracy at the Pentagon,” not the war with Iran.
Massie brought eight articles of impeachment against the defense secretary. The Kentucky congressman accused Hegseth of going to war with Iran without congressional authorization; continuing the war after lawmakers directed the withdrawal of U.S. forces; continuing to fight beyond the War Powers Resolution’s allowed timelines; ignoring laws to minimize civilian harm; directing the seizure of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife; retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., over his public statements; ordering deadly strikes against suspected drug traffickers at sea; and starting an illegal war in Yemen.
Hegseth briefly addressed the specific accusations, calling them “partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize our military.” He said none of the actions constituted high crimes, but rather “the job well done.”
“As for the articles themselves, Iran, the cartels, Maduro, Yemen — every one was a lawful operation ordered by the Commander in Chief, then ordered by myself, notified to Congress, and executed by American warriors who did their jobs,” Hegseth said.
The defense secretary praised the success of Operation Epic Fury — the U.S.’s campaign against Iran — claiming that Iran’s navy and more than 80% of its nuclear industrial base were destroyed. Hegseth also claimed that Iran started the war 47 years earlier.
Late last week, U.S. Central Command posted a plea on social media and a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran’s nuclear program.
Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, R-La., will decide if lawmakers vote on each article individually or all eight as a whole. Many Democrats have expressed support for Hegseth’s removal, as have some Republicans, who currently hold a slim majority in the House.
Representatives have two legislative days to vote. A simple majority in favor of impeachment would send the matter to the Senate for a trial, where a two-thirds majority would be required to convict and remove Hegseth.
There is no set timeline for an impeachment. If the House votes to impeach, the Senate’s trial could begin in the next legislative session, when Democrats take control of Congress.
Trump has been vocal about his support for Hegseth. On Monday, he called Massie a “loser” and a “sick guy,” saying, “There’s something wrong with him, actually. Now he’s after Pete Hegseth. He doesn’t like Hegseth, but really, what has Hegseth done?”
Massie lost his primary run for re-election to a Trump-backed contender in May.
Hegseth first announced the press conference while speaking with reporters Monday after delivering smoldering remarks against diversity, equity and inclusion efforts, as well as progressive academia, at the Naval War College in Newport, Rhode Island. He told reporters that the people who sought to remove him disagreed “with success,” later shifting the focus to the soldiers who carried out Pentagon policy decisions.
“If you want to take issue with what we did in Epic Fury or Rough Rider or nabbing Nicolás Maduro, you’re taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished, which is historic,” he said.
Before Tuesday, Hegseth’s most recent press conference was conducted May 5, amid the U.S.’s ongoing war with Iran.
The Unite for Veterans Coalition is hosting a gathering on the lawn of the U.S. Capitol to mark Veterans Day on Wednesday. There, veterans, family members and advocates plan to voice their support for Hegseth’s impeachment, organizers said.
Natalie Oliverio contributed to this report.

articles.title: Britain says its bases are safe after US refueling planes evacuated
articles.snippet: Commercially available flight tracking data showed at least 10 Boeing KC-135R Stratotanker refueling planes left the Royal Air Force base in Mildenhall, eastern England, on Monday.
articles.full_text:
LONDON — Britain said on Tuesday that its military bases were safe, after the U.S. removed huge refueling aircraft from a British airbase following what the Wall Street Journal said was a threat from Iran, the second such apparent evacuation in three months.
Commercially available flight tracking data showed at least 10 Boeing KC-135R Stratotanker refueling planes left the Royal Air Force base in Mildenhall, eastern England, on Monday. One flew to a base in Germany, one to Scotland and two to Spain, while the destinations of the other six were not reported.
At least three Osprey multipurpose aircraft also departed from Mildenhall and landed at Lakenheath, another RAF base 4 miles away. Video filmed by a member of the public from outside the base and verified by Reuters showed two Ospreys taxiing on the runway after landing at Lakenheath.
Asked about the moves, the U.S. European Command said the Air Force moves aircraft between locations for a variety of reasons, and it would not comment on force protection measures for operational security reasons.
A spokesman for Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the protection of Britain’s military bases was a top priority, and that the government worked closely with the police and allies to protect them.
Security measures were kept under constant review and the government was investing more than £2 billion ($2.7 billion) in air defense and counter-drone capabilities, he said. Asked if he was confident that Britain’s bases were safe, he said: “Yes.”
The White House and the Pentagon did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent outside regular business hours.
U.S. removed bombers
According to the Wall Street Journal, the evacuations were prompted by a threat from Iran. The precise nature of the threat was under discussion among U.S. officials, it said.
Iran has denied any links to specific attacks in Britain, but its Revolutionary Guards have said airbases used by U.S. forces there and in other countries are legitimate targets. Britain has been warning for months that Iran has been planning attacks, recruiting people online to carry them out.
In September, the United States removed bombers that had been used to strike Iran from another British base, RAF Fairford, on security grounds after a group of men approached the base in white vans.
Two men were charged last month in relation to that incident, with prosecutors alleging one of them had tried to assist Iranian intelligence in Britain.
Britain’s domestic spy chief Ken McCallum said in a speech last month that Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests over the past year. Iran was ramping up attempts to hit harder targets such as military sites in the U.K,, even though its previous activity had been limited by the lack of sophistication of the criminals it used as proxies, he said.
Upgraded security
The U.S. upgraded the security posture at RAF Mildenhall and another U.K. base, RAF Lakenheath, to FPCON Charlie, the second-highest defensive threat level, the WSJ report said, citing a U.S. official familiar with the matter.
The Fairford incident, which remains largely unexplained, attracted huge international attention at a time of heightened concern about the security implications for Western states of the war between the United States and Iran.
Burnham has said the activity at RAF Fairford was “highly likely” to have been coordinated in Iran.

articles.title: France orders military Earth-observation satellites for more than €1.5 billion
articles.snippet: France ordered two military Earth-observation satellites from Airbus and Thales Alenia Space for more than €1.5 billion (US$1.7 billion).
articles.full_text:
PARIS — France ordered two military Earth-observation satellites from Airbus and Thales Alenia Space for more than €1.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) to replace three existing orbiters, and to maintain a space-based image-intelligence capability beyond 2035.
The new satellites in the IRIS system will have an improved operational performance in terms of quality and the speed of making images available compared to the current CSO satellites, France’s Directorate General of Armament said on Monday. They’ll be able to take extremely high resolution images day and night in both the visible and the infrared spectrum around the world, the DGA said.
France is one of the few European NATO members with a sovereign constellation of high-end optical spy satellites, with many allies relying on lower-resolution assets and intelligence supplied by the United States. French President Emmanuel Macron said in January that France was providing two thirds of the intelligence capabilities supplied to Ukraine.
“The IRIS program aims to ensure the continuity of this capability while improving performance to meet the needs of the forces in a rapidly evolving strategic environment,” the DGA said.
The contract represents a value of more than €1.5 billion for the entire consortium, Airbus said in a separate statement. Airbus said it will provide the satellite platforms, a “significant share” of the payload on the first satellite and be responsible for the ground segment, while Thales Alenia Space will develop the second payload, provide critical elements of the first and contribute to the ground segment.
The new system, called IRIS after the French abbreviation of Instruments for Space Intelligence and Imaging, will be operated by the Space Command within the French Air and Space Force, though the DGA said the program is “resolutely open to cooperation” to allow partner countries to access the system.
The first of the new satellites is planned to become operational in 2033, with both in orbit around 2035, according to the DGA. The three satellites in the existing CSO system, for Composante Spatiale Optique, were launched in 2018, 2020 and 2025, respectively.
The DGA said it notified Airbus Defence and Space and Thales Alenia Space of the satellite order on Nov. 5. Subcontractors include Lynred, Pyxalis, Sodern, Safran Reosc and Air Liquide Advanced Technologies, according to the DGA.
The first IRIS satellite will replace the existing CSO-1 and CSO-2 satellites to ensure continuity of France’s space-based imagery intelligence capability, Thales said in a separate statement. After the end of the operational life of the last CSO satellite, the second IRIS satellite will “significantly enhance” image-resolution performance, it said.
Technologies developed for the IRIS system include a “hyper-stable” telescope with active optics, ultra-sensitive high-speed digital sensors and AI-based image processing, according to Thales, which owns 67% of Thales Alenia Space, with the remainder held by Italy’s Leonardo.
IRIS will integrate “the most advanced optical instrument ever built in Europe,” Thales Alenia Space CEO Hervé Derrey said in the statement.
