articles.title: Dutch firm Optics11 in talks with navies on secretive underwater listening tech
articles.snippet: For underwater use, the company’s fiber-optic sensing can detect an oil tanker at 100 kilometers, the CEO said.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — Dutch startup Optics11 is in talks with dozens of navies about using its optical-fiber sensing technology for underwater monitoring and threat detection, with between five and ten navies already signed on as clients, Chief Executive Officer Paul Heiden said.
The company will have around 35 paid trials this year with navies testing its tech, Heiden told Defense News at the Euronaval maritime-defense exhibition outside Paris on Nov. 4. Those tests include several for the German Navy through various local defense-prime partners, as well as for Sweden, the United Kingdom, Belgium and France.
Optics11 beams light through optic fiber to detect acoustic vibrations underwater, either for static monitoring or towed array sensors, and Heiden said the technology is more sensitive and has higher resolution than passive sonar using piezoelectric detection. The firm is developing a towed array for the Royal Netherlands Navy for the future Orka-class submarines ordered from France’s Naval Group.
“Every navy knows that this is the technology of the future,” Heiden said.
The Optics11 portfolio includes OptiBarrier, a stationary seabed monitoring system, and OptiArray, a towed array that can be deployed from submarines and unmanned vessels.
The CEO said Optics11 will probably raise funds next year, and do so at a unicorn valuation, referring to a startup valuation that exceeds US$1 billion. The startup raised around €100 million in funding in the past 15 months, through equity financing as well as €25 million in venture debt financing from the European Investment Bank, according to Heiden.
Optics11 is not yet profitable, and Heiden expects the company to become cash-flow positive in 2028.
The CEO said nearly everything around underwater data collection is “extremely secret” and a lot of information around navies using Optics11 technology is classified. He said the company’s products are currently deployed in war zones, “and yeah, I can’t say anything about that either.”
Optics11 has a technology lead in optical-fiber sensing after years of deep-tech research that would make it hard for a competitor to enter the market with anything similar, at least in markets including Europe, the Middle East and South East Asia, according to the CEO. He said he’s not sure where China or the United States stand in terms of developing similar technology.
The optical fiber technology used by Optics11 was initially used in medical applications, and is so sensitive it can detect cells dividing, according to Heiden. For underwater use, the company’s fiber-optic sensing can detect an oil tanker at 100 kilometers, the CEO said.
Most of the company’s “really crucial developments” of the past seven to eight years rely on trade secrets rather than patents to protect intellectual property, due to the sensitivity of the technology, Heiden said. The Dutch government provides specialists to help the firm protect its data, and vets company employees working on classified technology.
“You can’t publish this, you can’t patent it, so it all has to be kept secret, and we’re getting great help from the Dutch government to keep it truly secret,” Heiden said.
Heiden said he holds monthly discussions within the company to make sure employees disclose if, for example, they are being threatened or their families are being put under pressure.
The Optics11 strategy is to build and sell its products locally, both to reduce supply chain risk for customers and because governments want to see their defense investments flow back into their own economies. “We’ll identify who the local prime is, and then we’ll work with them to fully integrate our technology,” Heiden said.
Should Optics11 raise money next year, the funds would partly be used to finance its expansion in the Middle East and South East Asia, where the firm is opening offices and hiring staff with “the goal to operate in a highly localized manner.”
Optics11 already works with partners including Saab, Rheinmetall, Fincantieri, Thales and Exail, Heiden said. The firm is a technology supplier for Ocean Infinity, which was picked by the U.K. to manage the anti-submarine surveillance program as part of Britain’s Atlantic Bastion initiative.
The higher sensitivity of optical fiber compared to traditional sonar translates into a “much larger” amount of sensing data per cubic nautical mile, which Optics11 processes using its own edge-computing software, the CEO said.
“Initially I thought we could work with a partner, but our data density is so high that we couldn’t derive any value from third-party sonar processing software,” Heiden said. “That’s why we started building that kind of software ourselves, and it’s now an integral part of our offering. So we’ve really built a serious R&D operation here.”
Artificial intelligence has helped cut down the effort required to develop software, with Optics11 now employing ten developers, according to Heiden, who said that as recently as 2024 and 2025 he had still been planning for around 60 to 80 people in software development.
“That means you can invest that money in acoustic specialists who have a much better understanding of how sound travels through the ocean, which will allow you to optimize your algorithms much faster and make them more precise for sandy seabeds, rocky seabeds, that sort of thing,” the CEO said.
Optics11 has been working with the Royal Netherlands Navy for at least eight years, with the Dutch military providing millions of euros in subsidies, steering the direction of development, as well as testing the company’s technology on submarines, according to Heiden.
Attracting funding was still complicated for Optics11 in early 2024 due to financial firms excluding defense firms from investment portfolios, something which “completely changed” in November that same year after a vessel dragged its anchor in the Baltic Sea, severing several cables, Heiden said.
“All of a sudden all kinds of investment firms were willing to work with us,” Heiden said. “That was really driven by our ability to listen underwater, companies were prepared to seriously invest in that. So seriously, in fact, that over the last fifteen months we’ve raised about 100 million, which is quite a substantial amount.”

articles.title: Hegseth vows to fight impeachment ‘spectacle’
articles.snippet: “What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment,” Hegseth told reporters at the Pentagon this morning.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth came out swinging against a potential impeachment today, dismissing the charges introduced in the House yesterday as simple “policy disagreements.”
“What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability,” Hegseth told reporters at the Pentagon this morning. “It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.”
Hegseth’s comments — the first time he has appeared before press at the Pentagon in over 180 days — come less than 24 hours after Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against him. Massie, who lost his primary in May to a candidate backed by US President Donald Trump, has been an outspoken critic of the administration, and especially Hegseth, over an array of issues.
In the 34-page resolution [PDF] filed Monday, Massie charged the defense secretary with committing “high crimes and misdemeanors” and called him “a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office.”
Specifically, Massie cited eight articles for impeachment centering on:
- Violations of the War Powers Resolution of 1973 related to military operations against Iran;
- Ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties citing the US military strike on the Iranian elementary school that killed or injured more than 200 civilians;
- Suppressing free speech for retaliating on Sen Mark Kelly, a retired Navy captain, for appearing in a video advising service members of their duty to disobey unlawful orders;
- The kidnapping of a sovereign foreign leader associated with the abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro,
- Conducting an “unlawful” war in Yemen; and
- Extrajudicial killings tied to the strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Pacific waters.
“By subjecting persons merely suspected of criminal conduct to lethal military force without judicial process, without congressional authorization, and without establishing a lawful basis for treating such persons or vessels as military targets, Secretary Hegseth arrogated to himself and the Executive Branch the roles of judge, jury, and executioner and asserted a unilateral power to determine who may live and who may die,” the resolution said on the extrajudicial killings article of impeachment.
Hegseth defended military operations under his watch, calling them “lawful” and “successful.”
“I stand behind every one of these operations. I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow,” he said during Tuesday’s briefing.
Hegseth also seemingly previewed his defense strategy going forward, tying an impeachment as an assault on the troops that have been involved in the operations.
At a Monday press conference, Massie anticipated the move, asserting that removing the sitting defense secretary was a measure to protect them while saying that this was not about “war crimes.”
“This secretary has used our troops to go seize oil for large corporations in America,” Massie told reporters. “You shouldn’t be used like that, you signed up to pledge your life for this country.”
The House could vote on those articles of impeachment as soon as today and, if approved by a simple majority, those could be sent to the Senate for a trial under the current GOP leadership or next year when Democrats take control.
For now, Trump is publicly backing his sitting defense secretary, taking to social media this morning to write, “‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman.”
The House has only impeached two cabinet secretaries: Secretary of War William Belknap in 1876 and Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024. (Though Hegseth refers to himself as the Secretary of War, his official title remains Secretary of Defense.)
This is not Massie’s first call to impeach Hegseth. In September, he announced plans to force a vote in the House to impeach Hegseth and had been waiting for Congress to return after the mid-term elections to again push the issue.
As Republicans suffered a historic midterm defeat and the prospect of Massie pushing the impeachment came, news reports emerged suggesting Hegseth’s job could be in jeopardy. At the time Trump told reporters he was not considering replacing Hegseth, but suggested Hegseth would be “very popular” if he became a Senator and took over Sen. Marsha Blackburn’s office when she moved into the Tennessee governor’s mansion.
But later in the week, reports began emerging that Blackburn was not considering appointing Hegseth to her vacant Senate seat.
Around the same time, the Pentagon’s official social media account kicked into high gear to defend Hegseth. It first released a five-plus minute a video of Hegseth standing outside the Pentagon defending the Iran war and denouncing the “sham articles of impeachment.”
“Their policies don’t work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents,” he said on the video posted on X. “It’s all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me.”

articles.title: Korean Air Aerospace pushes forward with Collaborative Combat Aircraft plans
articles.snippet: “We delivered our CCA platform last year and will having flight tests at the end of this year,” Director of International Business for KE-ASD Haneul Kim confirmed.
articles.full_text:
DAEJEON, South Korea — Korean Air Aerospace Division (KE-ASD) is readying its Low Observable Wingman Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle System (LOWUS) loyal wingman drone to make its first flight by the end of this year, the company has announced.
During a visit to KE-ASD’s research and development facility in South Korea at the end of October, executives briefed media on the research and development activities conducted by the specialized aerospace and defense manufacturing business unit of Korean Air airline. That included discussing LOWUS, which the company plans to enter as its contender for South Korea’s upcoming Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) competition.
Like other media outlets, Breaking Defense accepted travel and accommodations from KE-ASD to attend the briefing.
“We delivered our CCA platform last year and will having flight tests at the end of this year,” Director of International Business for KE-ASD Haneul Kim confirmed, adding that that two technology demonstrator aircraft have been handed over to South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development (ADD).
Following the initial trials, LOWUS, which has a length of 10.4 meters (34.1 feet) and a wingspan of 9.4 meters, will enter a full-scale development program that is due to begin in 2029 to meet the anticipated South Korean government’s timeline for the CCA competition. The Korean government has not indicated when the competition will start, but the eventual CCA winner is expected to be deployed alongside manned platforms and later production blocks of the KF-21 fighter.
A 5,500-lbf turbofan engine being developed by the ADD and Hanwha is expected to be ready in 2032 for use with the LOWUS, enabling the CCA to fly at speeds of up to Mach 0.8 and stay aloft for up to three hours. This will replace the Ukrainian AI-222 engine that is powering the initial aircraft.
Jung told reporters that LOWUS will be equipped with an Active Electronically Scanned Array Radar and Electro Optical systems, with its initial mission set being reconnaissance and eventually expanded to include penetrating contested airspace ahead of manned aircraft for strike and other combat missions.
AI Pilot Program
On the software front, ADD has launched a project to develop an AI Pilot that will have AI-enabled air combat technologies, and Jung added that there are plans to retrofit and integrate the system into the LOWUS aircraft currently under development for flight demonstration.
KE-ASD has also invested significant effort into the development of AI-enabled drone swarm software, with the company successfully demonstrating its efforts in September at the 2026 Defense Drone Tech Fair in South Korea.
“A fleet of 22 drones autonomously carried out coordinated reconnaissance, high-maneuver swarm flight and precision strike missions, managed through Korean Air’s proprietary integrated battle management system,” said a KE-ASD social media post about the September demonstration.
Video from the event showed 22 drones moving into two separate swarms, with one acting as decoys to occupy a simulated adversary air defense system while the other swarm conducted an attack against a preset target by crashing into it in rapid succession.
“The system does more than provide voice updates based on a pre-set scenario: it uses AI to assess mission status in real time and communicate relevant updates. It can also retrieve drone status and weather information in response to user queries, making it optimized for operations in the field,” the post added.
KE-ASD’s Senior Manager for Systems Integration Sumno Jung said the technology demonstrators will be used for the flight tests which will then lead to Manned-Unmanned Teaming (MUM-T) trials with an ADD-operated KT-1 turboprop trainer that is scheduled to begin at the end of 2027.

articles.title: Army fields launched effects to 11 of 12 divisions, with Griffon Aerospace delivering the majority
articles.snippet: In line with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s 2025 Drone Dominance memo, the Army was directed to provide each headquarters division and multi-domain task force with launched effects.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Army has fielded launched effects to all but one of its headquarters divisions, with Griffon Aerospace supplying the majority of the systems, according to senior Army officials.
The unmanned systems have been delivered to 11 of its 12 HQ divisions and each multi-domain task force (MDTF), according to Lt. Col. Hunter Gray, product manager for launched effects under Program Acquisition Executive Maneuver Air. He told reporters Thursday that the effort is part of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s 2025 Drone Dominance memo, which directed the Army to provide each HQ division and MDTF with launched effects by the end of 2026.
The service plans to start providing the 12th and final division with launched effects next month, Gray said. He did not disclose what divisions have been fielded thus far, and the Army did not respond to queries on the matter by press time.
Launched effects are unmanned aircraft or payloads deployed from crewed aircraft, ground vehicles or maritime platforms to deliver various kinetic and non-kinetic capabilities. Depending on their range and payload, the systems can extend the reach of units and provide effects without putting personnel directly in harm’s way.
To meet its fielding goals, the Army turned to established industry partners with the capacity to deliver “mission-ready platforms” at scale, while leveraging commercial supply chains to keep up with demand, Gray said.
“That fit very well in alignment with the ongoing acquisition reform and the directives that we’ve seen in the robotic and autonomous systems space,” he said.
Ski Horrocks, the deputy program manager of unmanned aerial systems under PAE Maneuver Air, said Thursday that, in addition to the Army’s recent acquisition reform, industry has been able to provide launched effects at scale thanks to the DoD’s drone marketplace.
“The real magic behind the marketplace is all the rapid acquisition authorities and the contract vehicles,” he said. Because Other Transaction Authorities (OTAs) allow contracts to be awarded much more quickly than traditional FAR-based contracts, he explained that they have helped the Army “move fast” in scaling launched effects and other drone platforms to soldiers. OTAs are the go-to contract vehicle the Army uses to award vendors a spot on the marketplace.
Gray said that some vendors have been able to scale faster than others, with dual-use company Griffon Aerospace standing out because of both the demand for its systems and its ability to incorporate soldier feedback and deliver updated platforms shortly thereafter.
“That is the vendor that we’ve been able to scale the most based off of priority,” Gray said. Griffon is currently able to provide hundreds of systems per month to the Army, he added.
“From the time that we identified the need to scale to the time that the first tranche of systems was delivered was about three weeks,” Gray said, referring to Griffon’s systems. “Since then, we’ve continued to maintain a frequency of that feedback loop with that tech insertion cycle and [have] ordered more aircraft per cycle so that we can continue to responsibly scale the industrial base to demand.”
Gray did not disclose the total number of launched effects systems that have been delivered, but said the “majority” have been long-range capabilities provided by Griffon. Neither he nor Griffon President Jordan French would disclose all of the company’s platforms that have been fielded, but both said the Army has received systems from Griffon’s broader family of launched effects, including its Outlaw drone.
“To narrow in on a singular platform is not really how we look at acquiring systems,” Gray said.
The Army is also procuring a range of payload capabilities for its launched effects, rather than prioritizing one particular mission area. Gray said those include intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, electronic warfare and kinetic effects.
“The great thing about the way that these systems are designed and the way that they operate is that we can adjust the payloads based off of the user requirement in near real time,” he said. “The demand ebbs and flows based off of the concept of the operation of the unit that we’re dealing with.”
The comments come after the Army’s lead for Drone Dominance, Col. Gregory Merkl, told reporters in September that the service has enough systems to outfit each squad with small, one-way attack drones. However, the systems have not yet reached every squad, and the service lacks enough trained personnel to operate them, Merkl added.
As part of Hegseth’s Drone Dominance initiative, he mandated that every Army squad be equipped with small, one-way attack drones by the end of fiscal 2026. Merkl’s September comments suggest the service had not yet met that goal, despite having sufficient systems in its inventory.

articles.title: AI company Fireworks says hackers stole data, billing info during October breaches
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Fireworks said the incident affected a “limited number of customer accounts” — all of whom were notified of the attack.
articles.full_text:
AI company Fireworks says hackers stole data, billing info during October breaches
AI infrastructure company Fireworks said cybercriminals stole billing information and AI-specific data during two breaches last month.
Fireworks published an updated notice on Monday saying it hired Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 to investigate a data breach it initially discovered on October 6. The San Mateo-based company was founded in 2022 and has more than 10,000 customers, offering an array of AI systems and tools to companies.
Investigators found that a well-known, financially motivated cybercriminal group launched the attack and stole account and billing information as well as secrets — confidential digital pieces of information that grant access to human users or apps and allow them to communicate or perform actions. Fireworks said the incident affected a “limited number of customer accounts” — all of whom were notified of the attack.
Monday’s alert from Fireworks also notes that the company experienced another incident on October 23 where a third-party cloud provider that hosted their R&D machines was attacked by cybercriminals.
“On October 24, the unauthorized third party used [the provider] to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact,” the company said.
The hackers gained access to internal Fireworks data, billing information, invoices and payment history as well as datasets and other AI-related data.
The customers that were impacted have been notified. Fireworks is working with Palo Alto Networks on hardening its security posture and revoking compromised credentials.
Digital workspace company Notion released its own notice that some of its customers were impacted by the Fireworks breaches. The company said it was notified of the incident on November 2 and disconnected its systems from Fireworks, deleting all data in the Fireworks system.
“On November 6, Fireworks notified us that malicious actors may have accessed potential customer data. Our team immediately began another internal investigation,” the company said.
“We used Fireworks for classification jobs to help customers understand their own AI usage through a feature in Notion called Insights, and we used them as a general inference provider to serve open-weight models inside our product. The Insights feature has been disabled as we investigate this incident, and we are no longer serving open-weight models through Fireworks.”
LLMJacking
Fireworks said its breaches are part of a larger string of attacks recently spotlighted by incident responders at Google. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant published a blog last week about a tactic known as "LLMJacking” where hackers hijack an enterprise’s access to large language models.
Mandiant said it has responded to multiple LLMJacking incidents in 2026 spanning a variety of cloud and LLM providers while impacting “organizations in North America, South America, and Asia Pacific across the financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors.”
“Unlike the gradual resource consumption associated with cryptojacking, LLMJacking can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges in a matter of hours,” the researchers explained.
“Across individual incidents, we observed fraudulent charges associated with resource consumption exceeding $100,000 in a single day, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million before access was revoked.”
GTIG said it has identified a "diverse set of financially motivated threat clusters operating out of multiple regions globally" that are responsible for the attacks.
The groups are also maturing — with some focusing on initial access before handing off to other groups that monetize and resell the unauthorized access to large language models.
Multiple investigations showed the groups were primarily trying to steal tokens or credentials which allow threat actors to establish footholds into target organizations' infrastructure.
“As enterprises integrate higher-tier models and agentic workflows into production environments, cybercriminals will likely refine automated reconnaissance to target exposed API tokens and exploit vulnerabilities in model routing middleware,” GTIG said.
“This operational specialization will sustain a growing illicit resale marketplace, allowing threat actors to rapidly siphon enterprise quotas while passing the billing costs to victims before compromises are detected.”
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: Cybercriminals are increasingly infecting regular people with spyware
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Cybercriminals are infecting devices on a large scale with spyware, increasingly compromising systems belonging to average people, according to a new report.
articles.full_text:
Cybercriminals are increasingly infecting regular people with spyware
Cybercriminals are infecting devices on a large scale with spyware, increasingly compromising systems belonging to average people, according to a new report from the threat hunting firm iVerify.
The company found a rate of 1.07 spyware infections per 1,000 consumer scans of the startup’s free online checks.
The security firm reported a lower rate of infections for enterprises, detecting .7 infections per 1,000 scans, a disparity iVerify attributed to enterprises’ enforced patching, on-device detection and network security controls.
Company co-founder Rocky Cole declined to say exactly how many consumer devices the firm tested, but said hundreds of thousands were scanned. An average Fortune 500 company experiences about 65 infections per year on its devices, he said.
Notably, a large number of enterprise employees found with infected devices were rank and file workers as opposed to top executives.
“The takeaway is that this is the year that iOS spyware went mainstream and became everyone's problem,” Cole said. “The number one threat actor using spyware targeting iPhones these days is not governments; it's just cyber criminals, and it's a problem that is indiscriminate.”
Many of the device infections iVerify detected were used for credential and crypto theft as opposed to the more politically driven abuses often seen when advanced commercial spyware is deployed.
Attacks were carried out by bad actors using leaked iOS exploit toolkits to “work at scale, delivering attacks through online ads, reaching ordinary employees, and erasing their traces before defenders could respond,” according to the iVerify report.
About 75% of detections involved criminal actors deploying Coruna or DarkSword exploit kits, the report said. The other 25% were infected by mercenary spyware such as Pegasus.
DarkSword is an advanced, full-chain JavaScript-based iOS exploit kit and spyware framework first made public in March.
Deployed as a “watering hole” attack, DarkSword allows users to be infected without clicking on a link. Simply visiting a compromised website through a web browser can trigger the attack.
Coruna is also delivered via web-based attacks, where people visiting malicious sites trigger WebKit and kernel vulnerabilities. The spyware framework was purloined from a defense contractor and has been used by cybercriminals to facilitate the theft of cryptocurrency from over 42,000 iOS devices using fake Chinese-language financial websites.
The Google Threat Intelligence Group first discovered the Coruna exploit kit in February 2025 and it slowly proliferated across last year.
It has been directly tied to the actions of a former L3Harris Trenchant executive who pleaded guilty to stealing exploits and selling them on the black market in exchange for crypto payments. The executive, Peter Williams, was sentenced to seven years in prison in February 2026.
As with DarkSword, iVerify’s report said, Coruna is part of a “broader trend where mobile exploit frameworks… have shifted from rare, highly restricted intelligence operations into wider circulation.”
Owners of the devices infected with DarkSword and Coruna did not receive Apple threat notifications, the report said. Both exploit frameworks offer the same level of phone takeover as advanced commercial spyware brands like the zero-click Pegasus exploits and can expose messages, photos, emails and turn on microphones and cameras. The difference is that a broad population can access DarkSword and Coruna, whereas Pegasus and other commercial brands are exclusively sold to nation-state clients.
“One in 900 is a dragnet number, not a targeting number,” Nic Adams, co-founder and CEO of cyberkinetics company 0rcus said about the survey’s infection rate. “Mercenary spyware was built as a scalpel — now it’s being used as a net.”
Android is confronting a similar shift, the report said, as a large supply of inexpensive and turnkey spyware kits are letting bad actors easily take over phones from afar.
“The primary goal of these attacks isn't to steal intellectual property or get a leg up in trade negotiations — it's just cybercrime. Every single employee and every single person is potentially at risk,” Cole said.
The firm’s researchers had expected to find a decline in the rate of detected spyware infections this year since the number of average consumers using the free device checks quadrupled, Cole said. Two years ago, many of the people getting their devices checked were elites with reasons to suspect potential spyware.
An iVerify report published in December 2024 found Pegasus infections on 2.5 per 1,000 devices scanned. Coruna and DarkSword were not in the marketplace at the time and nation-state sponsored attacks using advanced commercial spyware were seen as by far the predominant threat. .
“Businesses need to update their threat models to stop focusing on VIPs and just assume this is a problem that everyone in the organization has to tackle,” Cole said.
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: Palantir exec nominated to lead CISA; lame-duck Senate vote is uncertain
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Michael LoSapio, Palantir's chief information security officer, is officially President Donald Trump's pick to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
articles.full_text:
Palantir exec nominated to lead CISA; lame-duck Senate vote is uncertain
President Donald Trump has nominated the chief information security officer of Palantir to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, potentially marking a turning point for an organization that has endured massive staff cuts and years of Republican attacks in recent years.
The president selected Michael LoSapio on Monday as the next head of the top civilian cyber defense agency, which has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since Trump returned to the Oval Office. A previous nominee, Sean Plankey, withdrew from consideration earlier this year after spending months in limbo on Capitol Hill; Nick Andersen has led CISA in an acting capacity since February.
The Homeland Security Department’s cyber wing lost more than 1,000 personnel — one-third of its workforce — and has seen its budget slashed by billions during the second Trump administration, following years of GOP complaints that its efforts to combat online disinformation during elections singled out conservative voices and infringed upon free speech rights.
As a result, CISA remained largely behind the scenes ahead of last week’s midterm elections. However, a spokesperson said the organization “provided voluntary, no-cost services” like vulnerability scanning ahead of Election Day and activated its Incident Coordination Group to serve as a threat information sharing hub.
It is unclear if the Senate will take up LoSapio’s nomination during the already jam-packed lame duck session of Congress, with lawmakers looking to approve a must-pass government funding measure and the annual defense policy bill, among other priorities.
Should lawmakers adjourn next month without approving his nomination, Trump would have to nominate LoSapio again next year for consideration by the incoming Democratic majority. A spokesperson for Sen. Rand Paul (R-KY), the chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
If the nomination is resubmitted next year, LoSapio could face increased scrutiny due to his role at Palantir, a software and artificial intelligence company with ties to the Trump administration. LoSapio joined the firm in 2017, leading its infrastructure and network security group before becoming CIO in late 2024, according to his LinkedIn profile.
Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-MS), who is expected to retake the reins of the House Homeland Security Committee, has signaled he plans to conduct thorough oversight of all DHS components, including CISA.
Andersen is widely seen as an effective leader and is well-liked. His temporary term expired September 24 based on federal statute limiting how long acting directors can stay in place. He remained on the job afterward through a bureaucratic move. By nominating LoSapio, the administration starts the clock again.
A former government cybersecurity official said via text that it is hard to know what to make of the LoSapio selection, “with the nomination coming out right at the beginning of the lame duck and exactly at the same time as Nick Andersen needed this to happen in order to remain Acting Director.”
LoSapio’s name had been floated several months ago, the former official said, but he questioned whether the administration would really push for him to be confirmed in 2026 and stick with him in 2027.
Other AI and cybersecurity experts said that while LoSapio’s background at Palantir gives him a unique perspective at a time when AI is becoming increasingly embedded in national security and every day cyber operations, that perspective isn’t sufficient for running CISA.
“There’s a big difference between securing a company that builds AI-powered technology and understanding how to defend against AI-driven threats” and running CISA, said Chris Cochran, who is vice president of AI Security at the SANS Institute.
“What I’ll be watching for is whether he can bridge that gap, particularly as we move toward autonomous attacks, AI agents, and adversaries operating at machine speed.”
Editor's Note: Updated 12:15 p.m. Eastern time with comments from experts.

articles.title: Russian hackers compromised government email servers to steal NATO, EU correspondence
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Russian state-linked hackers have compromised government email servers in Romania and Kazakhstan  to secretly intercept messages exchanged with NATO and European Union officials, researchers said.
articles.full_text:
Russian hackers compromised government email servers to steal NATO, EU correspondence
Russian state-linked hackers compromised government email servers in Romania and Kazakhstan using new malware to secretly intercept messages, including emails exchanged with NATO and European Union officials, according to research published Tuesday.
Slovak cybersecurity firm ESET attributed the campaign to Turla, a long-running Russian espionage group linked to the country's Federal Security Service (FSB).
The hackers used a previously unknown toolkit dubbed Cereal to monitor email traffic, steal specific messages and maintain access to compromised Microsoft Exchange servers without being detected.
“The Cereal toolset is a carefully constructed instrument for long-term, stealthy cyberespionage. It leaves little on disk, avoids external infrastructure that could be discovered and blocked, and conceals itself within legitimate Exchange processes,” ESET said.
The researchers said they first discovered the toolkit in November 2025 on a government email server in Kazakhstan and later identified it at a Romanian government organization.
In Romania, the malware was configured to collect emails exchanged with NATO and EU institutions. The attack came amid rising tensions between Russia and NATO over the war in Ukraine, including repeated incidents involving Russian drones entering or approaching Romanian territory.
In Kazakhstan, ESET said the intrusion took place amid growing scrutiny of Russian exiles and Kremlin critics living in the country. However, researchers could not determine whether the hackers were specifically seeking information about dissidents.
The campaign stands out for its unusual approach to concealing the hackers' activities, researchers said. Rather than relying on separate servers to control the malware, the attackers used the victims' own compromised Exchange servers to issue commands and manage the operation.
This allowed the hackers to operate without relying on external servers that security researchers could detect, block or shut down.
"Abusing a compromised Exchange server as a central operational hub is a rare technique, used by only a handful of APT groups," ESET said. "Turla has used variations of this approach in the past."
One component of Turla's new toolkit, called CerealBox, was embedded directly into a Microsoft Exchange service responsible for processing email traffic. It allowed the attackers to identify and capture messages of interest as they passed through the server.
According to ESET, the technique has not previously been documented in other malware families and demonstrates the attackers' detailed knowledge of Microsoft's email infrastructure.
The researchers could not determine how the attackers initially gained access to the government servers or how much information they obtained.
Also known as Secret Blizzard and Venomous Bear, Turla has operated since at least 2004 and is considered one of Russia's most established state-linked hacking groups. The group has a long history of targeting government agencies, diplomatic missions and defense organizations across Europe, Central Asia and the Middle East.
According to ESET, roughly 70% of the countries targeted by Turla since 2022 have been former Soviet republics or European countries with historical ties to the Soviet Union.
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Data breach at hearing aid giant Amplifon impacts thousands
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The U.S arm of international hearing aid company Amplifon has been notifying customers about a data breach early this year that included medical information.
articles.full_text:
Data breach at hearing aid giant Amplifon impacts thousands
International healthcare company Amplifon said thousands of its U.S. customers had their Social Security numbers and medical information stolen during a cyberattack in February.
The Milan, Italy, company pairs patients in need of hearing aids and auditory assistance with device providers and services.
Amplifon began notifying state regulators of a data breach last week, telling Texas officials that 85,804 people were impacted by the security incident in addition to 1,027 people in Vermont. The company also filed breach notices in California.
In a breach notice on its U.S. website, Amplifon said it initially discovered suspicious activity on February 11, with an investigation later revealing the hackers had access to company files between January 18 and February 8.
The stolen data includes names, driver’s licenses, state IDs, medical information, health insurance data and financial information.
No hacking group has taken credit for the incident as of Monday.
Several class action law firms said the total number of victims is 1,332,826, but Amplifon did not respond to requests for confirmation.
Amplifon was founded in 1950 for World War II veterans suffering from hearing loss and expanded to the U.S., Asia and Africa — now covering more than 28 countries across five continents. The company works with patients to find the right hearing devices and offer tests as well as other hearing-related healthcare services.
The healthcare industry, particularly companies producing wearable devices, has faced an unprecedented level of attack in 2026 by cybercriminals. Medical device maker iRhythm said last month that 8,179,772 people were impacted by a cyberattack on their systems.
Medical device makers like Medtronic, Boston Scientific, Stryker, UFP, Masimo, Surmodics, Artivion and Zoll have dealt with cybersecurity incidents that exposed the sensitive medical data of millions and caused supply chain issues.

articles.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
articles.snippet: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
articles.full_text:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.
The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.
Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.
Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.
“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.
“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”
All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.
As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

articles.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
articles.snippet: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user's Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet's access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
articles.full_text:
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).
The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”
The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.
Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).
The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.
Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.
Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.
Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.
In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.
Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.
That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.
Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linus Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links].
The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”
Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”
“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”
Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.
“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”
The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.
“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”

articles.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
articles.snippet: Expect to see quite a few websites serving "404" or "Page Not Found" errors today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
articles.full_text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.
Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.
OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”
Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.
Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].
“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.
The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.
According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.
“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”
The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.
This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.
Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

articles.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
articles.snippet: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
articles.full_text:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.
In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.
The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.
Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.
According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.
Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).
On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.
A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.
That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.
SHINYWIRE
KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.
The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.
The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.
Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).
In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.
The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”
Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.
GHOSTBYTE
According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.
A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.
“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”
It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.
Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).
In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.
“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”
The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.
CONFLICTING INTERESTS
It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.
Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.
In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).
But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.
That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”
